data.title: Corrected validity estimates reorder the selection methods, and work samples fall furthest
data.summary: Sackett et al. (2022) showed that the range-restriction corrections long used in personnel-selection meta-analyses systematically overstated validity, and re-estimated it. This paper reproduces the full table. Against the prior figures, the corrected operational validities are: structured interviews .42 (was .51), job knowledge tests .40 (was .48), empirically keyed biodata .38 (was .35), work sample tests .33 (was .54), general mental ability .31 (was .51), unstructured interviews .19 (was .38). Two readings matter here. Structured interviews become the strongest single predictor, ahead of general mental ability. And work sample tests fall furthest of anything in the table — .21 — so the familiar claim that a sample of the work is the best available signal no longer holds, though .33 still places it above general mental ability. These are correlations with job performance once hired. Nothing here measures whether a scoring scheme is applied consistently, published in advance, or opened at all.
data.citation: Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., & Lievens, F. (2023). Revisiting the design of selection systems in light of new findings regarding the validity of widely used predictors. Industrial and Organizational Psychology, 16(3). Reproducing the corrected estimates of Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens (2022), Journal of Applied Psychology 107(11), 2040–2068.
